title: Pulse-resolved post-generation phase control of squeezed light at 93 MHz with a bulk lithium-niobate modulator
authors: Edoardo Suerra, Igor Vasiljevic, Sebastiano Corli, Enrico Prati, Simone Cialdi
abstract: Time-domain multiplexing of continuous-variable quantum states provides a scalable approach to photonic quantum information processing, in which individual temporal modes can be sequentially manipulated within a common optical path. Here we demonstrate pulse-resolved post-generation phase control of squeezed-vacuum states at a repetition rate of 93 MHz using a low-loss bulk lithium-niobate electro-optic modulator driven by a broadband RF power amplifier. The driving architecture exploits low-cost, commercially available RF components and the impedance mismatch between the RF chain and the capacitive crystal load, rather than relying on dedicated custom high-voltage electronics, to obtain large voltage excursions on the modulator while operating above the piezoelectric-resonance region of lithium niobate. The modulator is driven synchronously with the optical pulse train, enabling the phase of consecutive temporal modes to be individually controlled. An interferometric calibration yields a maximum differential phase excursion of 1.93 rad. We apply the modulator to a 1035 nm squeezed-vacuum field generated by a synchronously pumped optical parametric oscillator and characterize the output using time-resolved balanced homodyne detection. With the local-oscillator phase kept fixed, the phase of the squeezed state is varied from pulse to pulse, and the corresponding phase-dependent quadrature variance is reconstructed. The resulting quadrature scan agrees with an equivalent measurement obtained by varying the local-oscillator phase with a piezoelectric actuator. These results demonstrate post-generation quantum-state phase control at the individual-pulse level and provide an electro-optic building block for programmable manipulation of time-multiplexed quantum states in recirculating optical architectures.
summary: This experiment demonstrates pulse-resolved phase control over squeezed-vacuum states using a bulk lithium-niobate electro-optic modulator operating at 93 MHz. By independently controlling the phase of successive optical pulses, the authors validate a key component for scalable, time-domain quantum information processing architectures. This technique allows for programmable manipulation of quantum resources in recirculating optical systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to demonstrate the ability to perform phase control on individual temporal modes of squeezed light, which is crucial for scalable photonic quantum information processing.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated pulse-resolved phase control of squeezed-vacuum states at a high repetition rate of 93 MHz, confirming the feasibility of post-generation quantum state manipulation.
method: They used a low-loss bulk lithium-niobate electro-optic modulator driven by a broadband RF amplifier to apply phase shifts pulse-by-pulse, followed by time-resolved balanced homodyne detection.
model_or_system: The system involves a synchronously pumped optical parametric oscillator generating squeezed-vacuum states at 1035 nm, which are then passed through the electro-optic modulator. The modulator's phase shift is controlled by an external, programmable electrical waveform.
key_observables: The phase-dependent quadrature variance ($\sigma_j^2$) of the squeezed state, measured via time-resolved balanced homodyne detection.
important_parameters: Repetition rate of 93 MHz; maximum differential phase excursion of 1.93 rad; detection efficiency ($\eta$) of 40%.
main_assumptions: The measurement relies on comparing the modulator-controlled scan against a reference scan achieved by varying the local-oscillator phase with a piezoelectric actuator.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the electro-optic modulator geometry and driving circuit, the overall experimental setup, and comparisons between the programmed phase modulation results and the PZT-scanned reference quadrature variance.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for time-domain multiplexing in QIP, details the use of the LiNbO$_3$ modulator driven by RF electronics, describes the time-resolved measurement protocol, and concludes by comparing the results to a known reference measurement.
why_interesting: This work provides a robust, high-repetition-rate electro-optic building block for programmable manipulation of time-multiplexed quantum states, directly advancing the hardware realization of continuous-variable quantum computation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Electro-optic phase modulator and electrical driv- ing circuit. (a) Geometry of the bulk lithium-niobate crystal. Gold electrodes deposited on opposite surfaces generate an RF electric field, ERF, oriented along the extraordinary crys- tallographic axis. The optical field propagates orthogonally to ERF and is polarized along the extraordinary direction. (b) Electrical circuit used to drive and monitor the crystal. The waveform generated by the arbitrary waveform generator (AWG) is amplified and transmitted to the crystal through a 10 m coaxial cable. A resistive voltage divider connected at the crystal input provides a monitor of the applied electrical waveform.

Figure 2. Experimental platform for pulse-resolved phase control of squeezed-vacuum states. A mode-locked laser operating at 1035 nm and 93 MHz provides the common optical and timing reference. A fraction of the laser output is frequency doubled in a lithium triborate (LBO) crystal and pumps the periodically poled lithium-niobate (PPLN) crystal inside the synchronously pumped optical parametric oscillator (SPOPO). The SPOPO generates a train of squeezed-vacuum pulses, denoted by QS. The state is transmitted through the bulk lithium-niobate phase modulator (LN) after its generation and is subsequently measured with a time-resolved balanced homodyne detector (HD). Figure 3. Electrical response of the bulk lithium-niobate phase modulator. The upper trace (blue) shows an example of a single modulation pulse generated by the AWG, while the lower trace (red) shows the corresponding voltage measured at the crystal input after RF amplification and propagation through the 10 m coaxial cable. A delayed reflected transient is observed at τ = 187 ns.

Figure 4. Interferometric calibration of the phase shift introduced by the lithium-niobate modulator. Panels (a)–(c) show representative electrical modulation pulses (red) and the corresponding optical interference signals (blue) for three different modulation amplitudes. The programmed AWG voltages are ±0.70 V, ±0.35 V, and ±0.10 V, respectively. Panel (d) reports the measured differential phase shift as a function of the voltage actually applied to the crystal. The solid line is a linear fit to the experimental data.

Figure 5. Pulse-resolved modulation and data-acquisition scheme. The optical pulse train, the electrical modulation waveform, and the synchronization signals are shown together with the corresponding organization of the acquired homodyne data. Each modulation pulse is associated with one temporal optical mode. The schematic example shows 7 phase settings for clarity, while the experimental sequence contains 15 consecutive temporal modes. The same sequence of phase settings is repeated N = 2000 times, allowing the homodyne samples corresponding to each phase setting to be collected over repeated measurements.
